rv.q: Still, with a vigil, a séance and jump scares that are the fun kind of frightening, this show is an entertaining ride.
"2:22" will be of most interest to connoisseurs of the heretofore generally shrinking stage-thriller genre, and those who want to fill their dance card with this fall's comparative bounty of options.
Danny Robins’s script is the likeliest to haunt your thoughts, both for its memorable performances and head-scratching dramaturgical liberties.

2:22 dramatizes those beats in more melodramatic fashion than Paranormal, with directors Matthew Dunster and Gabriel Vega Weissman seemingly encouraging their cast to play their characters to almost soap-operatic extremes.
Unfortunately, while the twist is clever, it’s also derivative — you’ve seen it before, done better — and it’s handled in such a rushed, cursory manner it fails to make the desired impact.
An impressively unsettling climactic twist can’t save this British import from its unconvincing characters and creaky plotting.
This spooky production offers way less in stage spectacle than The Lost Boys or Paranormal Activity.

Ultimately, directors Matthew Dunster and Gabriel Vega Weissman are more interested in the clever mechanics of their horror yarn — the jump scares, the wonky Alexa, the introduction of a cursed teddy bear — than in grounding it in a recognizable world of human beings placed in extreme circumstances.
For a play about listening for ghosts, 2:22 A Ghost Story never trusts silence long enough for anything to haunt you.

cn.t: This London import divides critics with its ghost story premise, earning praise for an unsettling twist but criticism for relying on loud jump scares over genuine atmosphere and tension.

vr.q: The payoff was fun. And, uh, I think it's kind of worth it for that... especially if you want something spooky light for your spooky season.
2:22 is an entertaining enough but hastily written story
